name: Native

hero.title: Build the website. Get the iPhone and Android apps.
hero.lede: PMTC compiles the components you build from Pyreon's primitives into SwiftUI for iOS and Jetpack Compose for Android. Your buttons, fields and lists become the platform's own views, with no JavaScript engine shipped to draw them. Experimental, and we mean it.

why.title: Not a web page in an app costume.

items.title: The platform's own views
items.text: A generated `Toggle` is the iOS toggle and the Android switch, so the next OS redesign reaches your app without a Pyreon release. `<Stack>` becomes `VStack` and `Column`; `<Field>` becomes `TextField`.

items.title: Signals become platform state
items.text: `signal()` and `computed()` compile to `@State` and `@Observable` on iOS, and `mutableStateOf` and `derivedStateOf` on Android. There is no re-render model to learn or work around, on the web or on the device.

items.title: Errors that name the problem
items.text: Code outside the native subset almost always gets a warning that names the construct and the file, often the line too, in milliseconds, before Xcode or Gradle runs. `--typecheck` adds a real `swiftc` pass on macOS.

items.title: Plain TypeScript keeps compiling
items.text: `effect()`, `setTimeout` and `setInterval`, `Date`, string and numeric `enum`s, `try`/`catch` and a typed `JSON.parse` now lower to Swift and Kotlin instead of stopping the build.

extraSectionsHtml:
how it ships

Three steps from TSX to the App Store build.

01

You write TSX

Primitives, signals and the Pyreon packages you already use on the web. One src/App.tsx.

02

PMTC compiles it

At build time the compiler emits Swift for iOS and Kotlin for Android. A construct it can't lower almost always gets a named warning, in milliseconds.

03

Xcode and Gradle build it

The generated source links against small Swift and Kotlin runtimes. What lands on the phone is a SwiftUI or Compose app. No JavaScript engine draws its screens.

runs on native today

The parts of your app that come along.

Anything bound to the DOM (a code editor, a rich-text editor) stays on the web, or runs inside a WebView with a two-way data bridge.

@pyreon/primitivesUI

The canonical primitives (22 in the next release) → SwiftUI and Compose views.

@pyreon/reactivitystate

signal, computed and effect → platform state.

@pyreon/routernavigation

Nested routes, guards, loaders and inbound deep links.

@pyreon/formforms

Validated forms, proven on device.

@pyreon/store · state-tree · machinestate

Stores, models and state machines.

@pyreon/i18n · permissionsapp logic

Translations and access rules.

@pyreon/storagepersistence

Persisted signals on the platform's own storage, on iOS and Android.

@pyreon/chartscharts

Every chart family, drawn natively.

@pyreon/hooksdevice

useClipboard, useColorScheme, useFetch, useOnline and more.

@pyreon/toastfeedback

A native overlay over the same toast() queue.

@pyreon/rxdata

Collection transforms lower to native operations.

Design Systemstyling

styled(), rocketstyle, Element and coolgrid patterns lower too.

the dev loop

Fast enough to stay in flow.

Measured on an Apple-silicon Mac with the iOS 18.5 simulator and the scaffolded app. pyreon-native check --watch answers "will this run on the device?" without opening Xcode.

under the hood

Six packages, all on npm.

The runtimes ship as Swift and Kotlin source through npm, so the Pyreon side of your native targets resolves from the same lockfile as the web app. npm create @pyreon/multiplatform@latest wires it all up.

@pyreon/native-compilerTypeScript

PMTC itself: TSX in, SwiftUI and Compose out.

@pyreon/native-cliTypeScript

The pyreon-native binary: build, check, dev, assets, wire.

@pyreon/native-runtime-swiftSwift

Core iOS runtime: tokens, HTTP, JSON, charts engine.

@pyreon/native-runtime-kotlinKotlin

The Android twin, plus storage backends.

@pyreon/native-router-swiftSwift

The router API on NavigationStack.

@pyreon/native-router-kotlinKotlin

The router API on Compose state.

api.title: Five names in your code, six packages underneath.

limits.title: Experimental, and the matrix says how much
limits.text: Each area is credited only for behaviour asserted on a simulator or emulator, and a CI gate keeps the headline equal to the table. Check it on the multiplatform page before you plan a release around it.

limits.title: A subset of TypeScript compiles
limits.text: Signals, typed props, the primitives, `<For>`/`<Show>` and the supported hooks lower. Run `pyreon-native check` while you write, and keep the rest in web-only files.

limits.title: No over-the-air code updates
limits.text: Native logic is compiled, so fixes ship through the stores. Data-driven config and `<WebView>` content are the ways to change behaviour between releases.

limits.title: A rebuild loop, not hot reload
limits.text: Native changes restart the app and reset in-memory state. Iterate on UI in the web build, where hot reload works.

limits.title: Packages compile only with a port
limits.text: PMTC lowers your source, not arbitrary npm packages. DOM-bound libraries stay on the web or run inside a `<WebView>`.

required CI checks on every native change: real Xcode and Gradle builds that run UI tests on an iOS Simulator and an Android emulator, plus Swift and Kotlin emit validation

comingFrom.title: A counter
comingFrom.note: Your JSX habits carry over; the component runs once and only the text updates. Expo is ahead where it counts for some teams: over-the-air updates (compiled native code cannot be patched that way), a much larger native SDK catalog and hosted builds. Pyreon gives you the platform's own SwiftUI and Compose views with no JavaScript engine, and a server-rendered website from the same source.

comingFrom.title: The same counter
comingFrom.note: Flutter draws its own pixels and leads on animation, desktop and maturity: its mobile targets are production, ours are experimental. Pyreon emits the platform's own widgets, so an OS redesign arrives for free, and the web build is real HTML with server rendering and SEO rather than a canvas.

recipes.title: A countdown on three platforms
recipes.text: Timers lower to a small `PyreonTimers` runtime: main-thread callbacks after at least `ms`, and on iOS the timer keeps firing while the user scrolls, as in a browser. Start it in `onMount` and return the cleanup.

recipes.title: State shared across components
recipes.text: Module-scope signals become one observable singleton for the file (`@Observable` on iOS, an `object` with `mutableStateOf` on Android), so every component in the file that reads them updates. The string `enum` becomes a native `enum`.

recipes.title: Import pasted JSON safely
recipes.text: `JSON.parse` with a cast becomes a typed, throwing decode (`JSONDecoder` on iOS, kotlinx-serialization on Android), and `try`/`catch` maps one to one. Malformed JSON lands in the `catch` on every target; natively the decode is stricter, so a wrong-shaped list lands there too.

faq.q: Is there a JavaScript engine on the phone?
faq.a: Not for your UI or your logic: the build is Swift and Kotlin source compiled by Xcode and Gradle. A `<WebView>` you place on purpose (to host a code editor, say) runs web content inside the system web view, like any native app's.

faq.q: Can I ship a store app with it today?
faq.a: The native targets are experimental. Screens that are mostly forms, lists, navigation and data are the strong part; heavy animation and a long list of third-party SDKs are not. The matrix on the multiplatform page states what is proven on a device.

faq.q: What happens when I write something it can't compile?
faq.a: You almost always get a warning that names the construct and the file (often the line too), from `pyreon-native check` or the editor through `pyreon-native check --lsp`. It does not try to run unsupported code on the device.

faq.q: How do I call a native SDK it doesn't wrap?
faq.a: Write a Swift or Kotlin class in your app and call it with `useNativeModule('Name')`. Member calls pass straight through, so Xcode and Gradle type-check them. It is more glue than installing an Expo module.
For iOS, yes: Xcode builds the app, and `--typecheck` needs `swiftc`. Android builds with Gradle on any machine with the Android SDK, and the web build runs anywhere.
